lesson_title: Three Loops, Two Rainy Seasons, One Country
hook_text: Cape Town's rain falls in winter. Joburg's falls in summer. Same country — here's why.
clip_script: Picture the space between the equator and the South Pole as three revolving doors stacked side by side. Door one sits over the tropics: the sun cooks the equator all year, air shoots straight up, dumps its rain, and drifts poleward high overhead. By the time it reaches about 30 degrees south — the Kalahari, the Namib — it has cooled and grown heavy, so it sinks. And sinking air is drying air. That is why the world's biggest deserts sit in a ring at 30 degrees. Door two is the lazy one in the middle latitudes; it does not turn itself, it gets pushed by its neighbours, and its wind is the westerlies that hurl cold fronts at Cape Town. Door three sits over the pole, freezing air creeping outward until it slams into the westerlies and the two shove each other upward. Now the trick that explains our whole country. Those belts are not nailed down. They slide north and south chasing the sun, by about five degrees. In winter everything slides north, so the cold fronts reach the Western Cape — Cape Town's rain arrives in June. In summer everything slides south, the fronts retreat out to sea, and wet tropical air pushes down into Limpopo and Gauteng. One sliding blanket, two completely different rainy seasons.
visual_style: Three glowing rotating loops drawn beside a cutaway globe from equator to pole, deserts lighting up as a ring at 30 degrees, then the whole belt system sliding north and south over a map of South Africa as the months tick past.
pacing: Steady build through the three loops, then a quick seasonal slide with month labels flying by.
